cells.tense: The practice is here, in your hands, and you are adding to it now.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: At the gathering, handle your own share of the work fully — all of it, no passing the heavy part to someone else mid-way. Stay with that piece to its end.
cells.core:
What began as wanting something has become standing with it, and you still stand — at the gatherings, doing the unglamorous parts, expecting neither thanks nor a finish line. The strength isn't a burst anymore; it's daily, and it's yours.

That kind of holding can tip over. When the practice matters this much, it's easy to shoulder pieces that aren't yours and call it devotion. Your own share is already the whole of it. At the gathering, carry only what's actually yours — every bit of it, and nothing borrowed. The practice doesn't need you doing the rest, and what you're hoping for is alive enough without the heroics.
cells.sheetLine: The thing you kept is still keeping you.
cells.verb: Keep carrying a shared thing past the first hope that started it

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead, the shared thing will need defending, and you are already braced for it.
cells.act: write both sides of it on one page and close the page
cells.ask: Before a charged conversation about the practice, set the case for it and the case against it on one page, shut the page, and walk in with it closed.
cells.core:
The gathering, the conversation about how it should go, gets rehearsed in your head first, and what should be a handing-down becomes holding a line. Your people can feel the bracing; they may not have words for it, but the tone changes when the topic comes up.

Hope doesn't have to argue. Take one evening and put the case for this and the case against it on the same page, then shut the page. Walk into that room with it closed, and trust the showing-up to speak for itself. Nothing about this needs you to win the exchange to keep it.
cells.sheetLine: You're guarding it harder than it's being threatened.
cells.verb: Keep carrying a shared thing past the first hope that started it

cells.tense: The door to the practice is behind you, and you are still standing outside it.
cells.act: tend the resource with responsible care
cells.ask: Pick the smallest shared piece you can reach this week — a recipe that came down, one story, one call to someone who keeps it too — tend only that, and add nothing.
cells.core:
A stopped thing, and you stopped with it. Part of you is still at the doorway, deciding whether to walk in, while the people who keep it meet without you. Not a crisis. Just a standing-still, long enough that it's become a place.

What you're waiting to feel is not on the other side of a bigger decision. It's on the other side of one small tending. Pick the smallest piece of the thing you can reach this week — a recipe that came down, one story, a call to someone who keeps it too — and look after only that. Add nothing yet, expect no feeling from it. What grows back is not a decision; it's a hand returning to a familiar object, and it starts with one thing done with care.

cells.tense: All this time, the practice has been held together by your hands, and you call it just what anyone does.
cells.act: persist on your own reserves through the pressure
cells.ask: Through the hard stretch on the practice, keep going on what you have without polling others on how they're doing with it — then note that you made it through.
cells.core:
The private version is where this started: you kept something smaller because you wanted to. That's the same strength seen at close range — one person, no audience, no duty yet. It's still the shape of how this works when it's going well: the arranging, the calls, the small timely repairs, done because the thing matters and you can, with nobody keeping score.

Try that private version again. Through the hard stretch, carry the practice on what you have without checking how others are faring with it, and finish it. Afterwards, notice who held it upright — not the group, not the custom. Your own hands did.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that this person stays on in shared traditions out of hope rather than habit or duty — the signature says persistence through aspiration, the record doesn't say why they keep it. A reader could reasonably say 'I show up because I'd be missed, not because I still hope for anything,' and the core should still leave them something to use. The ask survives being wrong: it scales the care they already give the shared thing, so it's still doable if the hope is smaller than the reading thinks. The sentence serving the writer more than them is 'the same faith your people kept before you' — it flatters the frame and says something about their history the record can't support; cut it.
